chapters.summary: Majority Leader Abreu introduces Rabbi Steven Exter of Bayit Hebrew Institute of Riverdale, who delivers an invocation asking for wisdom, compromise, and peace for the City Council.
chapters.title: Rabbi Steven Exter delivers invocation

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: We will now have today's invocation, which will be delivered by Rabbi Stephen Ekster of Bayet Hebrew Institute of Riverdale, which is located at 3700 Henry Hudson Parkway in the Bronx.

utterances.speaker: Rabbi Steven Exter
utterances.text: I rise as a constituent, friend, and admirer of Councilmember Eric Dinowitz with the deepest thanks.

utterances.speaker: Rabbi Steven Exter
utterances.text: God who bestows your spirit upon all flesh.

utterances.speaker: Rabbi Steven Exter
utterances.text: Bring your blessing upon the elected legislators of this august body, the City Council of the great city of New York, upon its Speaker and Deputy Speaker, leaders and all members.

utterances.speaker: Rabbi Steven Exter
utterances.text: Grant our legislators the wisdom, strength, and moral force to faithfully represent their constituents and to hear their own inner voices

utterances.speaker: Rabbi Steven Exter
utterances.text: so that they might make laws that are fair and just for all citizens, enshrining their freedoms

utterances.speaker: Rabbi Steven Exter
utterances.text: and promoting their health, well-being, and flourishing as children of the creator of us all.

utterances.speaker: Rabbi Steven Exter
utterances.text: Grant our legislators the sacred chutzpah to reach across the aisle and forge compromises for the greater good.

utterances.speaker: Rabbi Steven Exter
utterances.text: For what unites us is truly greater than what divides us.

utterances.speaker: Rabbi Steven Exter
utterances.text: 25 years after the most hateful acts our city has known, and just two days before the Jewish holiday of Sukkot, the Feast of Booths,

utterances.speaker: Rabbi Steven Exter
utterances.text: in which Jewish tradition understands that the ultimate sukkah, the ultimate dwelling, is the Sukkot Shalom.

utterances.speaker: Rabbi Steven Exter
utterances.text: The canopy of peace.

utterances.speaker: Rabbi Steven Exter
utterances.text: We ask you, God, to guide our city's council members in making this city, New York City,

utterances.speaker: Rabbi Steven Exter
utterances.text: a canopy of peace and welcome for all its inhabitants, living free of prejudice and fear,

utterances.speaker: Rabbi Steven Exter
utterances.text: a model city for all cities, of civil discourse and civic friendship,

utterances.speaker: Rabbi Steven Exter
utterances.text: of righteousness and justice, of love and loving kindness, a city of peace.

utterances.speaker: Rabbi Steven Exter
utterances.text: Let us say, Amen.

chapters.summary: Eric Dinowitz thanks Rabbi Exter, describes his leadership at the Hebrew Institute of Riverdale, and moves for unanimous consent to spread the invocation in full upon the record.
chapters.title: Council Member Dinowitz moves to spread invocation and praises Rabbi Exter

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Thank you, Rabbi Ekster.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: I will now ask Councilmember Eric Dinowitz to spread the invocation on the record.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Majority Leader.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Rabbi Stephen Ekster serves as Senior Rabbi of the Hebrew Institute of Riverdale, the BITE, a large Orthodox synagogue in the Bronx known for inclusivity,

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: and welcome and community building for people of all backgrounds.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And it is very easy for anyone in a large group, a large congregation, to get lost, maybe not feel at home.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: But when the senior rabbi of the institution greets everyone with a warm embrace,

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: both figurative and literal.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: It means that everyone has a home in the Bite, and it is one of the most, and he is leading one of the most incredible congregations, I think, in our entire city.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: It is felt in the air every time I go to services there, every time I bring my

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: children there.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: His ordination is from Yeshivat Chovavei Torah, rabbinical school.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: He's a Bronx resident for 23 years.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: He's proud to call himself a New Yorker, and I am proud to call him a constituent, a constituent that I call on often to guide me

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: in Jewish matters, both large and small, even the tiny.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: of rabbinical questions, I know I can call on him on any time.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And I want to even thank him today for teaching us all a new term, sacred chutzpah, something I'd never heard.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And I make a motion for unanimous consent to spread the invocation in full upon the record.

chapters.summary: Speaker Julie Menin discusses the Council's Climate Week celebration, water quality testing law, and the Generative Canopy Project to map trees and address extreme heat in Hunts Point, East New York, Corona, and Elmhurst.
chapters.title: Speaker Menin highlights Climate Week and environmental initiatives

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: We will now have communication from Speaker Julie Minnin.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Good afternoon, everyone.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: On Tuesday, the council hosted a Climate Week celebration, and that was just one of a thousand events held in this city where more than 100,000 people

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: from around the world came together to advance solutions for a more sustainable and safer future.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: As activists sound alarms of despair, it's up to us as government officials to respond with action and play a leading part in the fight against climate change.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Back in April, the City Council passed a law to increase water quality testing and created an advisory board to develop a wildlife...

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: management plan.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And in this year's budget, we allocated funding to support Cornell Tech and launch the Generative Canopy

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Project, investing a quarter of a million dollars to protect New Yorkers from extreme heat and bring environmental justice to the streets that we walk on.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: In particular, this project is going to focus on three regions that will, and the first ones are Hunts Point and Longwood and Councilmember Sanchez's district, East New York and parts of Councilmember Banks and Nurses districts,

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Corona and Elmhurst in parts of Councilmember Thomas Henry, Krishnan's, and Wong's districts.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: The initiative is going to map the location of each tree in the five boroughs as well as the cooling effect that they have, which will inform where it's most effective to plant trees.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And these efforts serve as just one example of the many ways that we are working on building a safer and healthier city.

chapters.summary: Speaker Menin announces the largest Fair Fares expansion, making nearly 1.3 million New Yorkers eligible, and highlights Council Member Crystal Hudson's bill to streamline enrollment.
chapters.title: Speaker Menin discusses Fair Fares expansion and Intro 248

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: As part of the budget we passed in June, the council secured the largest expansion of Fair Fares program in its history.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: So that residents earning up to 200% of the federal poverty line will soon qualify for half-price transit discounts on the bus, on the subway, and on paratransit.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: This expansion now means that nearly 1.3 million New Yorkers can focus on where they're going and not if they can afford to get there.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: While this was

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: a major victory for transit affordability and something the council truly prioritized, we still recognize that there are unnecessary barriers to enrolling in the program.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: As I said in May during our Fair Fares oversight hearing, a 40% enrollment rate is a failing grade, especially for such a vital program.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: So among the bills that we're voting on today, one that Councilmember Crystal Hudson introduced will mandate a streamlined process to enroll in fare fares.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: This effort is even more important given that 340,000 additional New Yorkers are now eligible due to the expansion that the council pushed for in the budget.

chapters.summary: Speaker Menin highlights Council Member Pierina Sanchez's bill to extend the J-51 tax abatement for co-ops, condos, and rental buildings, benefiting up to 300,000 units and aiding retrofits.
chapters.title: Speaker Menin discusses J-51 tax abatement extension

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Another bill introduced by Councilmember Pierina Sanchez will extend the J-51 tax abatement for certain co-ops, condos, and rental buildings, benefiting up to 300,000 of them.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: This legislation will make it easier to preserve and retrofit our city's stock of aging buildings at a time when the cost of housing has truly skyrocketed,

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: making it more affordable to complete repairs without shifting the burden onto tenants.

chapters.summary: Speaker Menin announces over $25 million allocated to Bellevue Hospital to modernize and expand its adult psychiatric department, adding about 40 inpatient beds.
chapters.title: Speaker Menin announces $25 million for Bellevue Hospital psychiatric expansion

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Speaking of affordability, the council also had a very significant announcement yesterday.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: I was so thrilled that so many colleagues were able to join.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: We announced that we allocated more than $25 million to Bellevue Hospital to modernize and expand their adult psychiatric department.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Our funding is going to add approximately 40 inpatient beds, helping the hospital.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Councilmember Maloney, for leading the cheering on this.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: It's a very important project.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Helping the hospital fulfill its function as a primary psychiatric institution for lower Manhattan and really unparalleled in the city.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Last year alone, Bellevue treated more than 11,000 adult psychiatric emergency patients with that unit operating at 98% occupancy.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: No New Yorker should be forced to linger in pain during their most vulnerable moments, let alone in a crowded emergency room.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: They should be met with immediate care, and that's what this investment will help ensure.

chapters.summary: Speaker Menin notes National Opioid Awareness Day and World Heart Day, urging New Yorkers to talk to doctors and check the World Heart Federation website.
chapters.title: Speaker Menin recognizes National Opioid Awareness Day and World Heart Day

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: On the subject of health, Sunday was National Opioid Awareness Day, and Sunday the 29th is World Heart Day.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: 80% of premature cardiovascular deaths can be prevented by mitigating key risk factors.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: So talk to your doctor and check out the World Heart Federation website to learn more.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: So on your way in this morning, you may have noticed student art adorning the rotunda.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: This was all due to six student artists, so I'd like to thank the New York City Arts and Education Roundtable for setting this up.

chapters.summary: Speaker Menin recognizes brothers from Iota Phi Theta fraternity, founded in 1963, and thanks them for their presence and values of scholarship and leadership.
chapters.title: Speaker Menin welcomes Iota Phi Theta fraternity

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: We also have brothers from Iota Phi Theta here.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: On September 9th, 19...

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: 1963 at Morgan State College, 12 men formed the fraternity based on the values of scholarship, leadership, citizenship, fidelity, and brotherhood.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Since then, the organization has grown to over 300 chapters and has initiated over 75,000 members, making it one of the nation's largest predominantly African American social service fraternities.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: You are our future and we hope that you will pursue public service beyond college.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: So thank you so much for being here.

chapters.title: Speaker Menin celebrates birthdays of Council Members Louis and Banks

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: So happy birthday to Councilmember Farrah Lewis, who celebrates tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin

chapters.summary: Speaker Menin notes Sukkot begins at sundown tomorrow and wishes all Jewish New Yorkers observing a Chag Sameach.
chapters.title: Speaker Menin wishes Jewish New Yorkers a happy Sukkot

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And lastly, Sukkot starts at sundown tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: For seven days, Jewish people across the world will eat, relax, and recite blessings in their sukkahs.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: It's a joyous holiday celebrating the harvest time, and I want to wish all Jewish New Yorkers observing a Chok Samay.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: The council will disapprove an application by Cali Tejadas Bakery and Restaurant for a revocable consent to operate a sidewalk cafe in Councilmember Chanel Thomas-Henry's district.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Introduction 833, sponsored by Councilmember Sandy Nure.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: would repeal certain building setback restrictions along portions of Eastern Parkway between Rockaway Avenue and Bushwick Avenue.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin

chapters.summary: Speaker Menin describes Resolution 184 declaring Korean Cultural Awareness Day, Resolution 606 declaring Black Pride Month, and Resolution 607 declaring African Immigrant Heritage Month.
chapters.title: Speaker Menin outlines resolutions on Korean Cultural Awareness, Black Pride, and African Immigrant Heritage

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Today, we will also vote on the following pieces of legislation.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Resolution 184, sponsored by Councilmember Amanda Farias, would declare October 3rd as Korean Cultural Awareness Day

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: annually in the City of New York to commemorate the mythological beginning of the Korean people and to celebrate their continued pride in their shared ancestry.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Resolution 606, sponsored by Councilmember Althea Stevens, would declare the month of August as Black Pride Month in the City of New York,

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: recognizing the legacy of New York City Black Pride movement of uplifting the Black LGBTQIA plus community and its continuing contributions to creating a more equitable New York City.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Resolution 607, also sponsored by Councilmember Althea Stevens, would declare the month of September as African Immigrant Heritage Month in the City of New York

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: to celebrate the contributions made by African immigrants to New York City and to the United States.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Thank you to Regina Paul.

chapters.summary: Pierina Sanchez discusses the housing and climate crises, the need to retrofit aging buildings, and the changes to the J-51 program extending it through 2036 and increasing cost recovery to 100%.
chapters.title: Council Member Pierina Sanchez speaks on J-51 tax abatement extension

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you, Majority Leader, and thank you, Speaker.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: We are facing a housing crisis and a climate crisis at the same time, and our aging buildings are at the center of both.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: These buildings are among our largest sources of greenhouse gas emissions, even as they break down around us.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Elevators are failing, stranding seniors and people with disabilities.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Roofs, boilers, electrical systems, and other critical infrastructure need investment.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: And in the Bronx and Queens, we're living the deadly consequences of aging housing and fire hazards.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: While government has a responsibility to set high standards for owners to keep buildings safe, protect tenants, and reduce emissions, we must also help owners make the investments that are being asked of them.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: The J51 program is one of the city's key financial tools to do just that, with $212.7 million spent by New York City in 2026.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: This program helps building owners keep up with the cost of necessary preservation work and upgrades, including installing energy-efficient systems so buildings can comply with Local Law 97.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Earlier this year, the state authorized the city to extend J51 with three key changes.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: First, a 10-year program.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: This one will go through June 2036.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Second, building owners will now be able to recover up to 100% of the reasonable cost of the rehabilitation, up from 70% in the past.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: And finally, co-ops and condos will...

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: see a raised assessed valuation cap from $45,000 per unit to $60,000 per unit, which may sound crazy to the average person, but remember these are Department of Finance assessed values.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: And these changes together bring the program's ability to expand the program's ability to reach 300,000 co-ops and condos citywide.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: 1015 maintains previous accountability mechanisms and adds new comprehensive reporting to how it's being used so we can continue to improve the program.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: I want to thank the Green Co-op Council, State Senator Brian Kavanaugh, and Assemblymember Edward Bronstein for their leadership on this bill in the state, and of course the Housing and Buildings Committee staff and my staff.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: And if I, yep, want to thank Dylan Campos, our incredible fellow, for all of his work on this and everything this past year.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Crystal Hudson explains her bills to streamline Fair Fares enrollment and require the Department of Correction to return commissary funds to people leaving custody, emphasizing government accessibility.
chapters.title: Council Member Hudson speaks on Intro 246 and Intro 248

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Councilmember Hudson.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Thank you so much and good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: I'd like to speak briefly on two of my bills that we're voting on today, Intro 246 and Intro 248.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Since entering office, I've advocated for policies that make it easier for New Yorkers to access the benefits and services they deserve.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: I got into public service to make government more accessible for more people.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Antiquated systems and unnecessary red tape make it nearly impossible for New Yorkers to reach benefits they're entitled to, and that fuels distrust in government.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Both of today's bills are about the same basic idea.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Government should return to people what is already theirs without an onerous process to obtain it.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Intro 248 bridges that gap.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: It creates a streamlined enrollment process for fair fares that allows DSS

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: to immediately enroll individuals with their consent into fair fares if they're also applying for SNAP or cash assistance.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Intro 246 also works to put cash into the pockets of New Yorkers by requiring the Department of Correction to tell every person in city jails exactly how much is in their account and directs the agency to return those funds via cash, check, or preloaded debit card

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: before the individual leaves custody.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Together, these bills send one message.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Whether it's benefits owed to a family or money owed to someone leaving custody, as government, we owe it to our constituents to ensure they get the money and benefits they are entitled to.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: I want to thank the advocates who have pushed for these reforms for years, including Writers Alliance, CSS, Permanent Citizens Advisory Committee to the MTA,

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Legal Aid Society, Freedom Agenda, as well as the teams at DSS and DOC, the Council's committee staff, and my team who helped get these bills across the finish line.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: We strengthen our children, our families, and our communities.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: I want to thank Senator Bailey and Assemblymember Diaz for championing this legislation in Albany and my council colleagues who have joined me in co-sponsoring this resolution.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Today, I proudly urge my colleagues to vote yes, and I urge our state partners to advance this legislation and governor to sign it into law.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Fatherhood matters, showing that matters, and every father who wants to be there for their child deserves support to do so.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.text: Thank you, Majority Leader.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: This morning, I joined council colleagues, state legislators, future members of Congress, including Brad Lander and Chris Rabb, and hundreds of New Yorkers in an act of civil disobedience to reject Prime Minister Netanyahu's visit to our city

chapters.summary: Lynn Schulman introduces Intro 1094 to lower the Legionella reporting threshold from 1,000 to 10 colony-forming units per milliliter, citing recent outbreaks and Canada's standard.
chapters.title: Council Member Shulman introduces Intro 1094 on Legionnaires' disease reporting

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Councilmember Shulman, followed by Thomas Henry.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Thank you, Majority Leader.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Today I'm introducing Intro 1094, which would strengthen our city's ability to help prevent outbreaks of Legionnaire's disease before they occur.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: This summer, New York City experienced two devastating clusters of Legionnaire's disease, reminding us of the serious health risks.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: that Legionella composed to New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Currently, building owners are only required to report Legionella test results to the Department of Health and Mental Hygiene when levels reach at least 1,000 colony-forming units per milliliter.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: But by the time Legionella reaches that level, an outbreak may already be imminent.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: This legislation would lower the reporting threshold to 10 colony-forming units per milliliter.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: This would give the department earlier notice of elevated Legionella levels, allowing the city to take action before conditions become dangerous.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: The testing level proposed in my legislation is a critical regulatory threshold across Canada.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: In fact, 10 bacteria per milliliter is the standard action level there.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: If a facility's cooling tower tests above 10 bacteria per milliliter, it triggers mandatory immediate decontamination and hyperchlorination protocols.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: This method has proven to be an effective, preventive, early warning line of defense.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: We should not wait until Legionella levels reach a point where an outbreak is imminent before the city has the information it needs to act.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: By requiring this new threshold, we can give the department a better opportunity to identify potential risks more quickly and intervene before people get sick.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: This legislation is about prevention and protecting the health of New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: After this year's clusters, we have an opportunity to learn from what happened and take steps to prevent the next one.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: And I also want to thank the Speaker for her leadership because we've had more legislation on Legionella this year than it did.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: any other time.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: So thank you.

chapters.summary: Shanel Thomas-Henry discusses New York hosting the World Cup, asks what happened to FIFA's promised $1 million legacy contribution, and introduces Resolution 655 urging FIFA to deliver it.
chapters.title: Council Member Thomas-Henry calls on FIFA to honor World Cup legacy contribution

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Thank you, Councilmember.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Councilmember Thomas Henry, followed by Banks.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Thank you, Majority Leader.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: We can all agree that summer 2026 will go down in history, but at the heart of it was New York welcoming the world.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: We opened our city, supported public safety and transportation, hosted watch parties, and invested nearly $90 million to make sure that the biggest sporting event in the world could have a home here in New York.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: But hosting an event of this magnitude cannot simply be about what New York gives.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: What my colleagues and I have been shouting from the rooftop is, how would an event of this magnitude benefit New Yorkers?

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: FIFA reportedly committed to providing host cities with a million-dollar legacy contribution to support soccer pitches and other community projects.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: That's $1 million invested directly back into our communities.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: That's a goal we hope all private partners will commit to.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: But now with an estimated $15 billion in FIFA revenue, we have to ask, what happened to the million dollars?

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: That money should have translated to the young person in Corona who deserves a safe field to play on.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: That money could have translated to park preservation where so many of our families celebrated this tournament together.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: And of course, it must translate to the small businesses and neighborhoods who preserve the culture and vibrancy of our corridors.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: My resolution 655 is simple.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: FIFA must honor its commitment and deliver a million-dollar legacy contribution promised to New York City.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: I urge my colleagues to support this.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Resolution.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: And last but not least, happy birthday, Parker.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Mommy loves you.

chapters.summary: Chris Banks introduces Bill 1072 to expand outreach for the rent increase exemption programs SCRIE and DRIE, add the Mayor's Office for People with Disabilities, and require annual training and reporting.
chapters.title: Council Member Banks introduces bill to expand SCRIE and DRIE outreach

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Councilmember Banks, followed by Farias.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Thank you, Majority Leader, and thank you, Speaker, to your leadership.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Today I'm introducing Bill 1072, which will expand the outreach and disability of the rent increase exemption, or DREE program, and the senior citizen rent increase exemption, better known as SCRI.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: This legislation will expand the city's existing requirements for the sharing information about SCRI to include DREE and add the mayor's office for the people with disabilities as a participating agency.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: It would also require the Department of Finance to provide an annual training to designated staff and participating city agencies

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: on eligibility requirements, application and renewal procedures, reasonable accommodations, program benefits, and applicant referrals.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Additionally, the Department of Finance would be required to report annually to the Council on these trainings and their outcomes.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: We are in the middle of an affordability crisis, and we hear about it, its effects on every corner of our city.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: It is our duty to do everything possible to protect New Yorkers who are especially vulnerable to rising housing costs.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: That includes our seniors, many of whom are retired and living on fixed incomes, as well as

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: people with disabilities and disabled veterans.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Scree and Dree provide meaningful relief by freezing the rent of eligible New Yorkers, helping them remain in their homes and communities.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: However, these programs can only help people if they know the assistance exists and understand how to access it.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: No eligible New Yorkers should miss out on this critical benefit simply because they never received the right informational guidance.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: By strengthening the outreach and improving the agency staff training and increasing accountability, this bill will help connect more eligible New Yorkers with the assistance they need to remain safely and affordably in their house.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Amanda Farías introduces Resolution 647 for Consent Awareness Week, Resolution 648 on defining consent in state law, Intro 1079 on the survivor hotline, and Resolution 646 declaring Hindu American Awareness Month.
chapters.title: Council Member Farías introduces four bills on consent, survivor hotline, and Hindu American month

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Councilor Farias, followed by Wilson.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Today I'm introducing four bills that I would like members to consider supporting.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: The first, Resolution 647, would establish Consent Awareness Week during the third week of September.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Consent affects how we respect one another's autonomy and boundaries, and education gives us a chance to build that understanding before someone is harmed.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Secondly, Resolution 648 calls on the state legislature to pass S-5521A-1140.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Consent appears throughout New York State's laws governing sexual offenses, but the penal law does not affirmatively define it.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: This legislation would establish a clear standard, a freely given, knowledgeable, and informed agreement by someone with the capacity to reason.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: The two resolutions work together, one advancing public education and the other calling for clarity in the

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: state law.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: I'm also introducing Intro 1079 concerning the survivor hotline operated by the mayor's office to end domestic and gender-based violence.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: It would require reporting on calls received and answered, wait times, interpretation needs, and referrals, among other measures.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: If people are waiting too long or leaving before they can access services, the city and this council should be able to see that and be able to respond.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: And finally, Resolution 646, which would declare October as Hindu American Awareness and Appreciation Month in New York City.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: This request came directly from constituents in District 18.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Hindu Americans come from many backgrounds, including communities like those in my district, and have contributed to our city's businesses, institutions, and cultural life.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: October offers an opportunity to recognize those contributions alongside the traditions and observances that make the month meaningful.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: I look forward to working with my colleagues to advance all four bills.

chapters.summary: Carl Wilson introduces the Pricing, Equity, and Transparency (PET) Act to require veterinary practices to disclose standard charges, provide estimates, and create a public website of average prices.
chapters.title: Council Member Wilson introduces PET Act for veterinary price transparency

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Councilmember Wilson, followed by Marano.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: Thank you, Majority Leader.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: One-third of New York City households have a pet, yet most New Yorkers cannot afford even a basic veterinary wellness visit.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: Veterinary prices have increased by 60% over the past decade, driven by the consolidation of the veterinary industry as private equity firms and large corporations purchase independent practices.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: Today, 50% of veterinary practices and 75% of emergency vet hospitals

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: are owned by large corporations, and pet owners are often unaware that a seemingly independent neighborhood practice is part of a larger chain.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: Pets are family, but rising costs have unfairly rendered pet care a luxury good.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: Tragically, some families face financial euthanasia, which is having to euthanize an animal because a treatable condition, they cannot afford the necessary treatment.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: My new bill, the Pricing, Equity, and Transparency, or PET Act, would require veterinary practices to clearly disclose and display standard charges and price ranges for commonly offered services.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: The PET Act will also require practices to provide written or electronic estimates for certain higher cost services upon request and provide itemized receipts.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: Additionally, the Department of Consumer and Worker Protection would establish and maintain a publicly accessible website to display average prices for common veterinary procedures.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: The PET Act will allow pet owners to compare prices, evaluate treatment options, anticipate expenses, and make more informed decisions about both their animal's care and the type of businesses they wish to support.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: By making it easier to shop around for veterinary services, the proposal would expand consumer choice, promote accountability and fair competition, promote more trusting relationships between vets and their clients, and help more New Yorkers access essential preventative and life-saving care.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: So thank you to the Ledge Division for their work on this, and I'm looking forward to working with my colleagues to pass this.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: Thanks so much.

chapters.summary: Frank Morano introduces Intro 1089 to create an Office of Assistance for 9/11 First Responders and Survivors, arguing they shouldn't have to navigate bureaucracy alone.
chapters.title: Council Member Morano introduces Intro 1089 for 9/11 first responders office

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Councilmember Marano, followed by Brewer.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Thank you, Majority Leader.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Twenty-five years ago, after the worst day in our city's history, New York made a promise that we will never forget.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: But never forget has to be more than two words that we say every September.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: And that's why today one of the bills I'm introducing is Intro 1089 to create an Office of Assistance for 9-11 First Responders and Survivors.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Because here's the absurd reality.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: A firefighter, a police officer, a construction worker, a volunteer, a downtown resident or survivor can spend years dealing with the consequences of September 11th

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: and then have to become an expert in government bureaucracy just to figure out where to turn for help.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: They survived September 11th.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: They shouldn't have to survive the paperwork, too.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: This office would give first responders and survivors a dedicated place in city government to help them navigate available services, benefits, and assistance.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: We're now a quarter century removed from September 11th.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: The ceremonies will become fewer.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: The headlines will become less frequent.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: But for thousands of New Yorkers, the consequences are in history.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: They're living them right now.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: They wake up with them every morning.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: So if we really mean never forget, let's put those words into law.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Let's make sure that when the people who were there for their city and when their city was in need, let's make sure their city is there for them.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: That's why I hope my colleagues will join me in calling.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Post-sponsoring, Intro 1089.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.text: But under the plan, Parks no longer accepts council funding or requests for new trees, eliminating a way to plant trees.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: So I wrote to Parks, and many of you signed the letter, asking the agency to continue accepting council funding and requests for trees.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Parks did not make that change.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: And that's why we have intro 1073.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: It restores a supplemental pathway without changing the neighborhood-based program.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: We can identify additional locations, and if it's feasible, we can plant a tree.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: This is additional money for additional trees.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Parks can continue prioritizing neighborhoods with the greatest need, while dollars can plant a tree in other locations.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: We all have to work together for this tree canopy, and we need every dollar.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Thank you to Chris Satori, Senior Legislative Counsel, for drafting this bill, and my Chief of Staff, Shula Puder.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: And let's make sure that the program, the neighborhood tree planting program, is not the only program for planting a tree.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Kayla Santosuosso introduces Intro 1058 to allow commercial tenants to recover legal fees if they successfully fight an eviction, leveling the playing field with landlords.
chapters.title: Council Member Santosuosso introduces Intro 1058 on commercial eviction legal fees

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Councilmember Santos Suoso, followed by Joang.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: Thank you, Majority Leader.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: I want to speak about my new bill, Intro 1058.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: Businesses across the city are struggling, including many historic institutions that bring untold value to our city.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: Despite that, our current commercial eviction laws often favor commercial landlords and often force beloved community institutions to close without ever seeing a judge.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: Currently, a commercial landlord can sue to evict a commercial tenant, and if they win in court, they can be reimbursed for their legal fees by the business in question.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: But in many of these contracts, the same is not true for the tenant.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: Even if they successfully fight off an eviction, a business...

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: Business often cannot have a way to make back legal fees that they have accrued in the process.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: The result is that landlords can encourage tenants to self-evict without ever having their day in court.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: This bill simply aims to level the playing field by creating a provision wherein a commercial tenant can recover their legal fees if they successfully fight off an eviction brought by a commercial landlord.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: It is a common sense bill which aims to give these tenants a fighting chance when they are faced with eviction and it is a much needed tool to keep these institutions open for years to come.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: I ask my colleagues to join me in supporting Intro 1058.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

chapters.summary: Susan Zhuang speaks about the Mid-Autumn Festival, sharing her immigrant experience and the traditions of mooncakes and family reunion, and wishes everyone a happy festival.
chapters.title: Council Member Zhuang recognizes Mid-Autumn Festival

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Councilmember Zhuang, followed by Hankerson.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Colleagues, today I want to recognize the Middle Autumn Festival, a holiday that means so much to me personally.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: I came to America as an immigrant when I was 20 years old, leaving behind my family, my home, everything I know.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: I know it feels like missing people you love and to be far away from your home.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: For generations, Chinese family have looked up at the moon during the holidays and remember the people they love.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: And we also burning fake money to the ancestors.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: We share the mooncake.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Because the circle represents family, reunion, and the togetherness, I want to thank Councilmember Phil Wong, brought a lot of mooncake today.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Colleagues, you haven't tried, you should try, but don't eat too much.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: New York City is very diverse.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Our differences are what makes us strong.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Every community brings our own traditions, stories, and hope.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: And together we make New York City the greatest city in the world.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: No matter where you travel, I want to wish everyone a happy Middle Autumn Festival and a happy Moon Festival.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: And try some mooncake.

chapters.summary: Ty Hankerson discusses Climate Week, the importance of trees and parks for cooling and stormwater management, and the disproportionate heat impacts on Black and brown communities.
chapters.title: Council Member Hankerson speaks on Climate Week and equitable tree canopy

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Councilmember Hankerson, followed by Narcisse.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Thank you, Majority Leader.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: This year, Climate Week comes with a heightened sense of urgency, as the United Nations has officially declared that the world will not meet the goals set by the Paris Climate Accord to cap rising temperatures at 1.5 degrees Celsius compared to pre-industrial levels.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: That is precisely why...

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: We need to invest even more heavily in reducing New York's carbon emissions and making our city more climate resilient.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: As Parks Chair, I see investing in our trees, parks, and various green spaces as one critical way that our city addresses a changing climate.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Our 7 million trees are crucial for keeping our city cool against rising heat.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: During the peak of summer, the temperature under a single tree canopy can be up to 25 degrees cooler than the surrounding street.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Our trees and parks also play a vital part in helping manage our city's stormwater, something we know all too well in Southeast Queens.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: As sea levels rise and flooding becomes more and more of a risk, our urban forest is a necessary tool for keeping people safe.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: But the reality is that these green assets are not distributed equally across New York.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: As our city continues to get hotter year after year, it will lead to lives being lost disproportionately in black and brown communities, which can be up to 10 degrees hotter due to a historical lack of foliage and green space.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Black New Yorkers already die of heat stress at double the rate of their white counterparts.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Without intervention, this number is sure to increase.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: I believe it's the duty of the council to be proactive and do everything within its power to mitigate the worst effects of climate change and to do so equitably.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: By building a greener infrastructure today, we can ensure that a resilient, thriving New York belongs to every single one of us tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Happy Climate Week.

chapters.summary: Mercedes Narcisse introduces Intro 1091 to require the Department of Buildings to notify homeowners when violations may result in a tax lien, protecting against loss of homes.
chapters.title: Council Member Narcisse introduces Intro 1091 on homeowner violation notifications

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Councilmember Narcisse, followed by Maloney.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Chair and Madam Speaker and the Deputy for bringing the package, Nantasha Williams, and I'm part of it.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Today, I'm proud to introduce Entry 1091 as part of the council package to protect our city's homeowners.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Too often, we see New Yorkers losing their homes, their lifeline investment, and path to building generational wealth over small little infraction building violations that spiral into

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: unconscionable death that we cannot control, uncontrollable death.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Not right and is not okay, like we would say, that these minor issues can lead to the devastating loss of families'most vulnerable assets.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: My bill takes a crucial step by requiring the Department of Building to proactively notify property owners when a violation on their property may result on a tax lien.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: If left unaddressed,

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: If left unaddressed, by equipping homeowners with this information early, we can help them take corrective action,

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: connect with resources, and prevent a crisis that threatens their home.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: As the affordability crisis put homeowners further and further out of reach for too many.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: This package of legislation demonstrates our commitment to supporting homeowners and preserving this vital pathway to stability and equity, which is the buzzword for so many.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: But when it comes to black and brown community, we need that equity in New York City and should be our commitment to keep the dream of home ownership alive for a generation of New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: And thank you, Madam Speaker.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: And I encourage all my colleagues to help me get this through.

chapters.summary: Virginia Maloney introduces legislation requiring large events to designate trained personnel and trauma-informed protocols for sexual harassment and assault prevention and response.
chapters.title: Council Member Maloney introduces bill on sexual assault prevention at large events

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Councilmember Maloney, followed by Kavan.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Thank you, Majority Leader.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: I am introducing legislation to strengthen sexual assault prevention and response at large public events across New York City.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: My bill would require events with more than 1,000 attendees or 500 when alcohol is being served to designate trained personnel

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: and establish clear trauma-informed protocols to prevent sexual harassment and assault and have a response when an incident occurs.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: If you're bringing thousands of people together for a concert, a festival, or a parade, you need a plan to keep them safe.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: I'm also proud to co-

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: co-sponsor, Councilmember Chanel Thomas-Henry's resolution number 655, calling on FIFA to show us the million bucks promised for hosting the World Cup.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Thank you again to Speaker Menon and my council colleagues for funding Bellevue in my district, supporting psychiatric help,

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: and again welcome New York City Arts and Education Roundtable, including Ian, who is a talented artist attending High School of Art and Design in my district.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Christopher Marte introduces Intro 1070 to provide contracted delivery workers unpaid safe and sick time without risk of punishment, building on previous delivery worker protections.
chapters.title: Council Member Marte introduces Intro 1070 for delivery worker sick time

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Councilmember Gawang, followed by Lewis.

utterances.speaker: Christopher Marte
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Christopher Marte
utterances.text: Each day, thousands of deliveristas move through our streets in heat waves, in storms, in intense city traffic, and they bring us our meals, they keep our city functioning.

utterances.speaker: Christopher Marte
utterances.text: And yet, when a deliverista or their family member gets sick or needs to seek shelter from violence, they face an impossible choice.

utterances.speaker: Christopher Marte
utterances.text: Take the time and be punished by the apps, or keep riding and risk their health and safety.

utterances.speaker: Christopher Marte
utterances.text: That's not a choice any worker in the city should have to make.

utterances.speaker: Christopher Marte
utterances.text: I'm introducing Intro 1070.

utterances.speaker: Christopher Marte
utterances.text: for flexible, safe, and sick time to give contracted delivery workers unpaid time off for their and their family's safety and health without the risk of punishment.

utterances.speaker: Christopher Marte
utterances.text: This council has really led the way on protecting delivery workers, whether it's providing for minimum pay, bathroom access, or the right to be treated with basic dignity.

utterances.speaker: Christopher Marte
utterances.text: And this bill represents a sensible continuation of that approach.

utterances.speaker: Christopher Marte
utterances.text: And it builds on our previous recognition that no worker should have to choose between a paycheck

utterances.speaker: Christopher Marte
utterances.text: and their health when we passed earned safe and sick time for employees.

utterances.speaker: Christopher Marte
utterances.text: So I urge all of you to join me as sponsor.

utterances.speaker: Christopher Marte
utterances.text: And I also want to recognize that several colleagues and I joined over 400 fellow New Yorkers in a Jewish-led civil disobedience, calling on our government to stop arming Israel amidst its ongoing genocide in Gaza.

utterances.speaker: Christopher Marte
utterances.text: We took this action as Prime Minister Netanyahu, a war criminal wanted by the ICC, speaks at the UN today and is embraced and funded by Trump.

utterances.speaker: Christopher Marte
utterances.text: It is time for elected officials to listen to the vast majority of Americans who demand that our federal government end its support for the Israeli military and fund people, not bombs.

utterances.speaker: Christopher Marte
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Farah Louis introduces Intro 1086 to expand the Alternative Enforcement Program to at least 400 distressed buildings yearly and Intro 1085 to increase fees for inspections and uncorrected violations.
chapters.title: Council Member Louis introduces bills to strengthen Alternative Enforcement Program

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Councilmember Lewis, followed by Nadineowitz.

utterances.speaker: Farah N. Louis
utterances.text: Thank you, Majority Leader.

utterances.speaker: Farah N. Louis
utterances.text: Today I'm introducing two pieces of legislation focused on tenant safety, accountability, and advocacy to make major long-needed improvements to the city's Alternative Enforcement Program, also known as AEP,

utterances.speaker: Farah N. Louis
utterances.text: both by expanding its reach and strengthening the consequences for owners who allow distressed buildings to remain poor in poor condition.

utterances.speaker: Farah N. Louis
utterances.text: Intro 1086 would expand the scope of AEP by requiring HPD to identify at least 400 distressed buildings each year, doubling the current statutory threshold.

utterances.speaker: Farah N. Louis
utterances.text: Importantly, at least 100 of these buildings must be properties that were previously discharged from the AEP program but have once again fallen into distress.

utterances.speaker: Farah N. Louis
utterances.text: The second bill, Intro 1085, addresses the other side of the equation, which is accountability.

utterances.speaker: Farah N. Louis
utterances.text: It would increase fees for inspections, monitoring, and other HPD actions, establishing minimum fees of $1,000 per dwelling unit.

utterances.speaker: Farah N. Louis
utterances.text: For building-wide inspections and monitoring along with additional fees when violations remain uncorrected.

utterances.speaker: Farah N. Louis
utterances.text: Together, these bills give the city more tools to identify distressed properties, bring more buildings under enhanced oversight, and create meaningful financial consequences for owners who fail to correct hazardous housing conditions.

utterances.speaker: Farah N. Louis
utterances.text: I look forward to...

utterances.speaker: Farah N. Louis
utterances.text: working with my colleagues, advocates, and the administration to advance these much-needed reforms and strengthen the AEP program as a whole.

utterances.speaker: Farah N. Louis
utterances.text: Our tenants deserve nothing less than a city government with the tools and enforcement mechanisms necessary to protect them.

utterances.speaker: Farah N. Louis
utterances.text: I encourage my colleagues to sign on to these bills.

utterances.speaker: Farah N. Louis
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Eric Dinowitz responds to earlier comments, disputing claims of genocide, arguing the term is used before and after military action, and defending Israel against what he calls demonizing language.
chapters.title: Council Member Dinowitz responds to genocide claims and defends Israel

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: And our last speaker is Councilmember Dinowitz.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I just have to say, after hearing some of the comments about visitors to the country, however you feel about those individual visitors,

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: you know, this word that I keep hearing, this genocide, this claim of genocide, is a claim that was made

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: before Israel even started retaliating against Hamas after October 7th.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: when they murdered and raped over a thousand people.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And it's just ridiculous to me that before the retaliation was claims of genocide, after

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: after a ceasefire, that same word is being used.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And the problem is, what does it do?

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: It obscures the actual issues that are going on there, the actual trauma and the actual destruction that is happening in the region.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: You are unable, we are unable to have a real conversation and really address actual policy issues because of the demonizing language that existed before there was any military action and after there is a ceasefire

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: in place.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And the demonization causes real harm.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And it is very specific to one country.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And the reason we know this, the reason we say we should stop doing any aid to Israel, is because the very same people saying that, out of one side of their mouth,

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: out of the other side say we should never sanction any country.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: We should never boycott from any country because that will only serve to hurt the citizens and the people who live in that country.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: But there is a special exception made for Israel and it is especially okay apparently to use this

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: demonizing language without evidence before the war begins and after the ceasefire is in place.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Thank you, Majority Leader.

summary: The New York City Council held a stated meeting on September 24, 2026, beginning with roll call, an invocation by Rabbi Steven Exter, and adoption of minutes.
Speaker Julie Menin delivered communications on Climate Week, Fair Fares expansion, J-51 tax abatement, Bellevue Hospital funding, and upcoming legislation.

The Council voted on land use items, finance resolutions, and several bills, then held general discussion where members introduced new legislation on topics including Legionnaires' disease, delivery worker sick time, and 9/11 first responder assistance.
